title: Honey as a Sweetener in Drinks
description: Honey sweetens tea, lemonade, and warm milk with a flavor that sugar cannot copy, because honey carries floral and caramel notes from the flowers the bees visited. It dissolves fastest in warm liquid, so stir it into hot tea or warm milk rather than shaking it into ice-cold drinks, where it clumps and sinks. The standard substitution is three quarters of a cup of honey for one cup of sugar, with other liquid in the drink cut back, because honey itself is about one fifth water. Honey is sweeter than sugar by volume, so a drink sweetened with honey needs less of it than the sugar version, and its flavor changes the drink rather than simply sweetening it.
ingredients: Honey (any mild variety for tea, stronger varieties for lemonade)
Hot water, tea, lemonade, or warm milk
Lemon juice or milk, as the drink requires
method: Heat the drink until it is hot but not boiling, since boiling drives off delicate honey aroma.
Pour the drink into a cup and add honey at three quarters of the sugar amount the recipe calls for.
Stir until the honey is fully dissolved and no streaks remain.
Taste and adjust with a little more honey or a squeeze of lemon, since honey varieties differ in sweetness.
For iced drinks, first dissolve the honey in a little hot water to make a honey syrup, then mix it cold.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat.
storage: Keep honey in a sealed jar at room temperature; it keeps for years but crystallizes over time, which is normal and reversible.
variations: Honey lemonade: dissolve honey in warm water, then add lemon juice and cold water.
Honey milk: stir honey into warm milk with a pinch of cinnamon.
Ginger honey tea: steep fresh ginger with black tea, then sweeten with honey.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey as a Sweetener in Drinks'
CUPS = [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
for sugar in CUPS:
    honey = sugar * 0.75
    liquid_cut_tbsp = sugar * 3
    print("%s cups sugar -> %.2f cups honey, cut liquid by %.0f tbsp" % (sugar, honey, liquid_cut_tbsp))
print("Rule: use 3/4 cup honey per 1 cup sugar, cut other liquid, lower oven by 25 F.")
demo.expected_output:
0.25 cups sugar -> 0.19 cups honey, cut liquid by 1 tbsp
0.5 cups sugar -> 0.38 cups honey, cut liquid by 2 tbsp
1.0 cups sugar -> 0.75 cups honey, cut liquid by 3 tbsp
2.0 cups sugar -> 1.50 cups honey, cut liquid by 6 tbsp
Rule: use 3/4 cup honey per 1 cup sugar, cut other liquid, lower oven by 25 F.

title: Honey Baking: Honey Cakes, Gingerbread, and Baklava
description: Honey baking covers cakes, gingerbread, and baklava, three traditions where honey is not a substitute but the defining ingredient. Honey cakes stay moist for days because honey holds water, and they darken faster than sugar cakes because honey sugars brown at lower temperatures, so honey cakes are baked cooler and checked early. Gingerbread uses honey or treacle as its binder and sweetener, giving the crumb its chew and its spice-carrying depth, while baklava brushes each layer of pastry with butter and finishes with a hot honey syrup poured over the hot pastry so the syrup soaks without making the layers soggy. In every case the rule is the same: less honey than sugar, less other liquid, a cooler oven, and an earlier check.
ingredients: Honey (mild for cakes, dark for gingerbread)
Flour, butter, eggs, and baking soda
Nuts and phyllo pastry for baklava
method: Measure honey by weight, not by cup, since honey is dense and sticky and cup measures vary.
For cakes, use three quarters of a cup of honey per cup of sugar, cut other liquid by three tablespoons per cup of honey, and add a quarter teaspoon of baking soda per cup of honey.
Lower the oven temperature by 25 degrees Fahrenheit compared with the sugar version.
Check the cake ten minutes before the recipe time; honey cakes look done at the edges while the center is still soft.
For baklava, bake the layered pastry until golden, then pour hot honey syrup over the hot pastry and rest it for at least four hours before cutting.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat.
storage: Store honey cakes wrapped airtight at room temperature for up to five days; store baklava uncovered at room temperature so the pastry stays crisp.
variations: Honey spice cake: add cinnamon, ginger, and orange zest to a plain honey cake batter.
Soft gingerbread: use dark honey and bake just until the center springs back.
Walnut baklava: layer chopped walnuts with cinnamon between phyllo sheets.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey Baking: Honey Cakes, Gingerbread, and Baklava'
BASE_HONEY_G = 240
SCALE = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
for s in SCALE:
    print("Scale %.1fx: honey %d g, flour %d g, soda %.1f tsp" % (s, BASE_HONEY_G * s, 300 * s, 1.0 * s))
print("Honey cakes brown faster: check 10 minutes before the recipe time.")

Scale 0.5x: honey 120 g, flour 150 g, soda 0.5 tsp
Scale 1.0x: honey 240 g, flour 300 g, soda 1.0 tsp
Scale 2.0x: honey 480 g, flour 600 g, soda 2.0 tsp

title: Honey Glazes and Marinades
description: A honey glaze is a thin, sweet coating brushed onto roasted meat, poultry, vegetables, or tofu near the end of cooking, and a honey marinade is the same idea applied before cooking so the flavor soaks in. Honey glazes work because honey sugars caramelize into a glossy, browned crust, but that same property means a glaze brushed on too early burns before the food is cooked, so glazes go on in the last fifteen minutes. A good glaze balances honey with something sharp, such as mustard, vinegar, citrus juice, or soy sauce, so the sweetness does not flatten the dish. Marinades add oil and salt to that balance, and the honey in them helps the surface brown while the acid and salt season the interior.
ingredients: Mustard, vinegar, citrus juice, or soy sauce
Garlic, herbs, or chili, as the dish requires
method: Whisk honey with mustard and a splash of vinegar until smooth; the standard glaze is about three parts honey to two parts mustard.
For a marinade, add oil and salt to the same mixture and coat the food, then rest it refrigerated for one to four hours.
Cook the food unglazed until it is nearly done.
Brush the glaze on in thin layers during the last fifteen minutes, turning and re-brushing so it builds a glossy coat.
Rest the food for five minutes before serving so the glaze sets rather than running off.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Never reuse a marinade that touched raw meat unless it is boiled first.
storage: Store unused glaze refrigerated for up to a week; discard any marinade that touched raw food unless boiled.
variations: Honey mustard glaze: honey, wholegrain mustard, and lemon juice for chicken and carrots.
Honey soy glaze: honey, soy sauce, garlic, and ginger for salmon and tofu.
Honey chili glaze: honey, vinegar, and chili flakes for roasted squash.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey Glazes and Marinades'
PER_KG_G = 60
WEIGHTS = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
for w in WEIGHTS:
    print("%.1f kg -> %d g glaze (%d g honey, %d g mustard)" % (w, PER_KG_G * w, PER_KG_G * w * 0.6, PER_KG_G * w * 0.4))
print("Brush glaze on in the last 15 minutes so the honey does not burn.")
demo.expected_output:
0.5 kg -> 30 g glaze (18 g honey, 12 g mustard)
1.0 kg -> 60 g glaze (36 g honey, 24 g mustard)
2.0 kg -> 120 g glaze (72 g honey, 48 g mustard)
3.0 kg -> 180 g glaze (108 g honey, 72 g mustard)
Brush glaze on in the last 15 minutes so the honey does not burn.

title: Mead and Honey Wine
description: Mead is wine made by fermenting honey and water with yeast, and it is one of the oldest fermented drinks in the world, predating grape wine in many cultures. The basic recipe is honey dissolved in water, yeast added, and the mixture left to ferment for weeks to months, with the honey-to-water ratio setting the sweetness and strength: a light hydromel uses about one part honey to four parts water, while a strong sack mead uses closer to one part honey to two parts water. Fermentation converts honey sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide, and the finished mead is racked off the sediment, aged, and bottled. Estimating alcohol before brewing uses the original gravity, measured with a hydrometer, and the final gravity after fermentation, with the difference multiplied by 131.25 giving an approximate alcohol percentage. Mead is an adult drink; it contains alcohol, and home fermentation must be done with clean equipment and an airlock so the fermenting liquid can release gas without letting in contaminants.
ingredients: Honey (any variety; wildflower is the classic mead honey)
Clean bottles and corks or caps
method: Dissolve the honey in warm water, stirring until no honey remains at the bottom, and cool to room temperature.
Pour into a sanitized fermenter, add yeast nutrient, and pitch the yeast.
Fit the airlock and ferment at 60 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit for two to six weeks, until bubbling slows.
Measure the gravity with a hydrometer; when it is stable over three days, rack the mead off the sediment into a clean vessel.
Age for at least three months, then bottle, label with the date and alcohol estimate, and store cool.
safety: Alcoholic drink for adults only. Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Sanitize all equipment; discard any batch that smells of vinegar or shows mold, and never seal a fermenting vessel airtight, since pressure can burst it.
storage: Store bottled mead upright or on its side in a cool, dark place; mead improves for one to three years and keeps well beyond that if sealed.
variations: Traditional mead: honey, water, and yeast only.
Melomel: mead fermented with fruit such as berries or cherries.
Metheglin: mead spiced with herbs such as cinnamon, clove, or ginger.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Mead and Honey Wine'
HONEY_KG = 3.0; WATER_L = 11.0; FG = 1.01
lbs = HONEY_KG * 2.20462; gal = WATER_L * 0.264172
og = 1 + (lbs * 35 / gal) / 1000.0
abv = (og - FG) * 131.25
print("Honey %.1f kg in %.1f L water" % (HONEY_KG, WATER_L))
print("Estimated original gravity: %.3f" % og)
print("Estimated ABV at FG %.3f: %.1f%%" % (FG, abv))
print("Estimate only: measure with a hydrometer; fermentation varies with yeast and temperature.")
demo.expected_output:
Honey 3.0 kg in 11.0 L water
Estimated original gravity: 1.080
Estimated ABV at FG 1.010: 9.1%
Estimate only: measure with a hydrometer; fermentation varies with yeast and temperature.

title: Honey Vinegar and Honey Beer (Braggot)
description: Honey vinegar is vinegar made by first fermenting honey and water into a weak honey wine and then converting that alcohol into acetic acid with a vinegar mother, a culture of acetic acid bacteria. The result is a mild, floral vinegar that works in dressings and marinades and carries honey aroma without honey sweetness. Honey beer, properly called braggot, is a different drink: beer brewed from malted grain and honey together, with the honey added during the boil or during fermentation so its sugars ferment alongside the malt. A braggot balances malt body with honey lightness, and its alcohol estimate comes from the combined sugars of malt and honey, measured the same way as mead, from original gravity to final gravity. Both products need patience and clean equipment, and both are adult products in the vinegar's case only by trace alcohol, since finished vinegar contains almost no alcohol.
ingredients: Honey and clean water for vinegar; malted grain and honey for braggot
Vinegar mother for honey vinegar; beer yeast for braggot
method: For honey vinegar: ferment honey and water with wine yeast into a weak wine, then add a vinegar mother and cover with cloth, not an airtight lid, so air reaches the culture.
Keep the vinegar vessel warm and dark for four to eight weeks, tasting weekly, until it is sharply acidic.
For braggot: brew a malt wort, add honey during the last ten minutes of the boil or at the start of fermentation, and ferment with beer yeast.
Measure original and final gravity to estimate alcohol, then condition the braggot for at least four weeks.
Bottle both products, label with dates, and store cool.
safety: Honey vinegar is acidic; do not use it as a medical treatment. Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Braggot is an alcoholic drink for adults only. Discard any batch with mold or a rotten smell.
storage: Store honey vinegar in sealed bottles at room temperature for a year or more; store braggot cool and dark, and drink within a year for the freshest honey aroma.
variations: Herb honey vinegar: steep thyme or rosemary in finished honey vinegar for two weeks.
Dark braggot: use dark malt and dark honey for a stout-like braggot.
Light braggot: use pale malt and light honey for a crisp, golden braggot.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey Vinegar and Honey Beer (Braggot)'
HONEY_KG = 1.5; MALT_KG = 2.0; WATER_L = 10.0; FG = 1.012
lbs_h = HONEY_KG * 2.20462; lbs_m = MALT_KG * 2.20462; gal = WATER_L * 0.264172
og = 1 + (lbs_h * 35 + lbs_m * 29) / gal / 1000.0
print("Honey %.1f kg + malt %.1f kg in %.1f L" % (HONEY_KG, MALT_KG, WATER_L))
print("Estimated original gravity: %.3f" % og)
print("Estimated ABV at FG %.3f: %.1f%%" % (FG, (og - FG) * 131.25))
demo.expected_output:
Honey 1.5 kg + malt 2.0 kg in 10.0 L
Estimated original gravity: 1.092
Estimated ABV at FG 1.012: 10.5%

title: Honey Confectionery: Honeycomb Candy, Nougat, Halva, and Honey Caramels
description: Honey confectionery turns honey into candy by boiling it with sugar to precise temperature stages, each stage giving a different texture. Honeycomb candy, also called sponge candy or cinder toffee, is made by boiling sugar, honey, and water to the hard-crack stage and then whisking in baking soda, which foams the hot syrup into a crisp, airy sponge that sets hard and shatters. Nougat whips hot honey syrup into egg whites to make a chewy, nut-filled bar, halva binds sesame or nuts with hot honey syrup into a crumbly, sliceable block, and honey caramels cook honey, sugar, cream, and butter to the firm-ball stage for a soft, chewy candy. The shared skill is temperature control: a candy thermometer is essential, because honey browns and burns faster than plain sugar syrup, and a few degrees change the texture completely. All four candies are adult-supervised projects around hot sugar, which can cause serious burns.
ingredients: Egg whites and nuts for nougat
Sesame paste or ground nuts for halva
A candy thermometer and a heavy pan
method: For honeycomb candy: boil sugar, honey, and water to 300 degrees Fahrenheit, remove from heat, whisk in baking soda quickly, and pour into a lined pan without stirring.
For nougat: boil honey syrup to 250 degrees Fahrenheit, whip egg whites to soft peaks, pour the hot syrup in slowly while whipping, then fold in nuts and press into a lined pan.
For halva: heat honey syrup to 240 degrees Fahrenheit and stir it into sesame paste or ground nuts until thick, then press into a lined pan.
For honey caramels: cook honey, sugar, cream, and butter to 245 degrees Fahrenheit, pour into a lined pan, cool, and cut into squares.
Cool every candy fully before cutting, and wrap pieces individually so they do not stick together.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Hot sugar causes serious burns: keep children away from the stove, use long sleeves and oven mitts, and never pour hot syrup near water.
storage: Store honeycomb candy airtight with parchment between layers, since humidity softens it; store nougat, halva, and caramels wrapped airtight at room temperature for two to four weeks.
variations: Chocolate-coated honeycomb: dip cooled honeycomb pieces in melted chocolate.
Almond nougat: use toasted almonds and a little orange zest.
Tahini halva: use tahini and honey only, pressed and chilled before slicing.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey Confectionery: Honeycomb Candy, Nougat, Halva, and Honey Caramels'
STAGES = [('Soft ball', 235, 245), ('Firm ball', 245, 250), ('Hard ball', 250, 265), ('Soft crack', 270, 290), ('Hard crack', 300, 310)]
BATCH_G = 500
for name, lo, hi in STAGES:
    print("%s: %d-%d F" % (name, lo, hi))
print("Batch %d g honeycomb candy at soft-crack needs %d g sugar base" % (BATCH_G, int(BATCH_G * 0.6)))
print("Use a candy thermometer; honey browns fast past 300 F.")
demo.expected_output:
Soft ball: 235-245 F
Firm ball: 245-250 F
Hard ball: 250-265 F
Soft crack: 270-290 F
Hard crack: 300-310 F
Batch 500 g honeycomb candy at soft-crack needs 300 g sugar base
Use a candy thermometer; honey browns fast past 300 F.

title: Honey Preserves: Honey-Preserved Fruit, Infused Honey, and Creamed Honey
description: Honey preserves fruit because honey is mostly sugar with very little free water, so microbes that need water cannot grow in it, and fruit stored under honey keeps for months. Honey-preserved fruit is made by layering clean, dry fruit in honey and sealing the jar, with the honey slowly drawing out fruit juice and taking on fruit flavor. Infused honey is the reverse idea: flavorings such as vanilla, cinnamon, chili, or herbs are steeped in honey for weeks, and the honey takes on their aroma while remaining honey. Creamed honey, also called whipped or spun honey, is made by seeding liquid honey with a small amount of finely crystallized honey and holding it cool, so it crystallizes into tiny, smooth crystals instead of large gritty ones, giving a thick, spreadable texture that never drips. All three methods depend on keeping water out, since added water lets honey ferment instead of preserving.
ingredients: Honey (liquid for preserving and infusing, crystallized seed for creamed honey)
Clean, dry fruit, herbs, spices, or vanilla
Sterilized glass jars with tight lids
method: For honey-preserved fruit: wash and thoroughly dry the fruit, layer it in a sterilized jar, and cover completely with honey, leaving no fruit exposed to air.
Seal and store cool and dark for at least four weeks, turning the jar weekly.
For infused honey: add the flavoring to liquid honey, seal, and steep for two to four weeks, tasting weekly and removing the flavoring when the taste is strong enough.
For creamed honey: stir one part finely crystallized honey into nine parts liquid honey, hold at about 57 degrees Fahrenheit for one to two weeks, and stir occasionally.
Label every jar with its contents and date before storing.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Keep all fruit and flavorings dry; wet fruit or herbs can ferment the honey. Discard any jar that bubbles, smells of alcohol, or shows mold.
storage: Store honey preserves sealed in a cool, dark place for six to twelve months; store creamed honey at room temperature and stir if it separates.
variations: Berry honey: preserve raspberries or blackberries under honey for spooning over yogurt.
Vanilla infused honey: steep one split vanilla bean in 500 g honey for a month.
Cinnamon creamed honey: whip a pinch of cinnamon into creamed honey for toast.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey Preserves: Honey-Preserved Fruit, Infused Honey, and Creamed Honey'
FRUIT_G = 400; HONEY_G = 600; SEED_PCT = 10
print("Honey-preserved fruit: %d g fruit in %d g honey (ratio %.2f:1)" % (FRUIT_G, HONEY_G, HONEY_G / FRUIT_G))
print("Creamed honey seed: %d g seed per %d g liquid honey" % (int(HONEY_G * SEED_PCT / 100), HONEY_G))
print("Keep infused honey dry: water invites fermentation.")
demo.expected_output:
Honey-preserved fruit: 400 g fruit in 600 g honey (ratio 1.50:1)
Creamed honey seed: 60 g seed per 600 g liquid honey
Keep infused honey dry: water invites fermentation.

title: Honeycomb and Comb Honey Eating
description: Comb honey is honey eaten exactly as the bees stored it, still sealed in the wax comb, and it is the most direct way to eat honey there is. A piece of comb is cut from the frame, and the eater chews it: the wax cells break, the honey flows out, and the soft wax can be chewed like gum and then spit out, or swallowed, since beeswax passes through the body undigested. Comb honey tastes different from extracted honey because the wax adds a subtle, clean texture and the honey inside has never been heated or filtered, so it keeps the full aroma of the hive. Good comb honey is fully capped, meaning the bees sealed every cell with wax, which shows the honey inside was ripe, and it is sold as a whole section, a cut piece in a container, or a chunk dropped into a jar of liquid honey. Eating comb honey needs no preparation beyond a knife and a plate, and it is best enjoyed plain, on warm bread, or with cheese, where its texture can be appreciated.
ingredients: A sharp knife and a plate
Warm bread or cheese, if serving with food
method: Cut a piece of comb from the section with a sharp knife, keeping the piece intact.
Place the comb on bread, on cheese, or directly on a plate for eating plain.
Bite or chew the comb: the wax breaks and the honey flows out.
Chew the wax briefly to press out the remaining honey, then spit the wax out or swallow it, as you prefer.
Wipe the knife and plate clean, since comb honey is sticky, and store any leftover comb covered.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Comb honey is raw honey: it carries the same infant botulism rule as any honey, and it should come from a trusted beekeeper, since it is unfiltered and unheated.
storage: Store comb honey covered at room temperature; if liquid honey is added to the container, the comb will slowly soften but keeps well for months.
variations: Comb on toast: a thick slice of comb on warm, buttered bread.
Comb with cheese: comb honey with a strong cheese such as blue or aged cheddar.
Chunk honey: a piece of comb dropped into a jar of liquid honey, sold and served together.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honeycomb and Comb Honey Eating'
FRAME_G = 1200; PORTION_G = 60
portions = FRAME_G // PORTION_G
print("One frame of %d g comb honey gives %d portions of %d g" % (FRAME_G, portions, PORTION_G))
print("Leftover: %d g" % (FRAME_G - portions * PORTION_G))
print("Chew comb, swallow the honey, and spit out or swallow the wax as you prefer; wax is not digested.")
demo.expected_output:
One frame of 1200 g comb honey gives 20 portions of 60 g
Leftover: 0 g
Chew comb, swallow the honey, and spit out or swallow the wax as you prefer; wax is not digested.

title: Honey Beverages: Honey Lemonade, Honey Tea Blends, Honey Milk, and Switchel-Style Drinks
description: Honey beverages are drinks where honey is the sweetener and part of the flavor, and they divide into four families that cover the whole year. Honey lemonade dissolves honey in warm water before lemon juice is added, so the honey never clumps in the cold drink. Honey tea blends sweeten black, green, or herbal tea with honey chosen to match the tea: mild honey for green tea, stronger honey for black tea. Honey milk stirs honey into warm milk, sometimes with cinnamon or vanilla, as a simple evening drink. Switchel-style drinks, the old farm drink also called haymaker's punch, mix water, vinegar, ginger, and honey into a tart, refreshing cooler that was drunk by field workers long before sports drinks existed. The shared technique is dissolving honey hot first, then finishing the drink cold or warm as the recipe requires.
ingredients: Water, tea, milk, lemon juice, or vinegar
Cinnamon or vanilla for honey milk
method: For honey lemonade: dissolve honey in a little hot water, then add lemon juice and cold water to taste.
For honey tea: brew the tea, then stir in honey while the tea is still hot.
For honey milk: warm milk gently, stir in honey and a pinch of cinnamon, and serve warm.
For switchel-style drinks: mix water, vinegar, grated ginger, and honey, stir until dissolved, and chill before serving.
Taste every drink before serving, since honey varieties differ in sweetness and flavor strength.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Switchel-style drinks contain vinegar; they are not suitable for young children in large amounts, and honey drinks are never for infants.
storage: Store leftover honey lemonade and switchel refrigerated for up to three days; make honey tea and honey milk fresh each time.
variations: Sparkling honey lemonade: top honey lemonade with sparkling water.
Iced honey green tea: brew double-strength, dissolve honey hot, pour over ice.
Ginger honey milk: add grated ginger to warm honey milk and strain before serving.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey Beverages: Honey Lemonade, Honey Tea Blends, Honey Milk, and Switchel-Style Drinks'
RATIOS = [('Light', 1, 1), ('Rich', 2, 1), ('Strong', 3, 1)]
for name, honey, water in RATIOS:
    total = honey + water
    print("%s syrup: %d parts honey + %d parts water = %.0f%% honey" % (name, honey, water, honey / total * 100))
print("Rich 2:1 syrup keeps longer; 1:1 syrup mixes cold drinks fastest.")
demo.expected_output:
Light syrup: 1 parts honey + 1 parts water = 50% honey
Rich syrup: 2 parts honey + 1 parts water = 67% honey
Strong syrup: 3 parts honey + 1 parts water = 75% honey
Rich 2:1 syrup keeps longer; 1:1 syrup mixes cold drinks fastest.

title: Honey in Savory Cooking: Mustards, Dressings, and Sauces
description: Honey belongs in savory cooking wherever a dish needs a small amount of sweetness to balance salt, acid, or heat, and its best savory roles are mustard sauces, salad dressings, and pan sauces. Honey mustard blends honey with mustard in roughly equal parts for a dip or sandwich spread, and the mustard's sharpness keeps the honey from tasting like dessert. In dressings, honey does two jobs: it sweetens, and it helps oil and vinegar stay mixed, since honey's thickness slows the dressing from separating. In pan sauces, a spoonful of honey added to the pan juices with stock or vinegar creates a glaze-like sauce that coats roasted vegetables, chicken, or pork. The rule in all three roles is restraint: one to two tablespoons of honey per batch is usually enough, and more than that turns a savory dish sweet.
ingredients: Salad leaves, vegetables, or cooked meat for serving
method: For honey mustard: whisk equal parts honey and wholegrain mustard with a squeeze of lemon juice.
For dressing: whisk honey into the vinegar first, then whisk in oil slowly until the dressing thickens and holds.
Season the dressing with salt and pepper and taste: it should be balanced, not sweet.
For pan sauce: after roasting, pour off excess fat, add stock and a spoonful of honey to the pan, and simmer while scraping up the browned bits.
Spoon the sauce over the dish and serve at once, since honey sauces thicken as they cool.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Refrigerate dressings and sauces promptly; discard any dressing left at room temperature for more than two hours.
storage: Store honey dressings refrigerated for up to a week; whisk or shake before using, since they separate when cold.
variations: Honey vinaigrette: honey, cider vinegar, oil, and Dijon mustard over green salads.
Honey garlic sauce: honey, garlic, soy sauce, and vinegar simmered for stir-fries.
Honey barbecue sauce: honey, tomato, vinegar, and spices simmered for grilled vegetables.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey in Savory Cooking: Mustards, Dressings, and Sauces'
OIL = 120; VINEGAR = 40; HONEY = 20
total = OIL + VINEGAR + HONEY
print("Dressing: %d ml oil, %d ml vinegar, %d ml honey = %d ml total" % (OIL, VINEGAR, HONEY, total))
print("Honey share: %.1f%%; oil share: %.1f%%" % (HONEY / total * 100, OIL / total * 100))
print("Whisk honey into the vinegar first; the emulsion holds longer.")
demo.expected_output:
Dressing: 120 ml oil, 40 ml vinegar, 20 ml honey = 180 ml total
Honey share: 11.1%; oil share: 66.7%
Whisk honey into the vinegar first; the emulsion holds longer.

title: Honey Wound and Skin Care, Evidence-Graded
description: Honey has been used on skin and wounds for thousands of years, and modern research has graded that traditional use with very different results for different claims, which is why this record grades each claim separately instead of praising honey as a whole. Medical-grade honey dressings, which are sterilized and standardized, have supported evidence for helping some minor wounds and burns stay moist and clean when used under proper wound care, and that support is for the dressing as part of care, not for honey alone healing a wound. Honey for cough has mixed-to-supported evidence in children over one year and in adults, where trials show it can soothe a cough about as well as some over-the-counter syrups, but it does not treat the infection causing the cough. Claims that honey cures infections, diabetes, cancer, or chronic disease are unproven, and honey must never be applied to deep, infected, or slow-healing wounds instead of medical care. Ordinary table honey is not sterile and is not a substitute for a medical-grade dressing. Honey is not a cure for any disease. Nothing in this record diagnoses, treats, or replaces medical care; see a clinician for wounds that are deep, large, infected, slow to heal, or on the face, hands, feet, or genitals, and for any cough that is severe, bloody, or lasts more than a few weeks.
ingredients: Medical-grade honey dressing (for the supported wound-care use only)
method: For minor skin care: wash the skin with clean water, pat dry, and apply a thin layer of honey only if the skin is unbroken and you are not allergic to bee products.
Cover with clean gauze if needed, and remove and wash off after a few hours.
For a cough in a person over one year old: a teaspoon of honey in warm tea may soothe the throat, following the same infant rule that honey is never for infants under 12 months.
Do not apply honey to deep, large, infected, or slow-healing wounds, and do not delay medical care to try honey first.
Stop and wash off the honey if the skin reddens, itches, or swells, which can signal an allergy.
safety: Honey is not a cure for any disease. Nothing in this record diagnoses, treats, or replaces medical care; see a clinician for wounds that are deep, large, infected, slow to heal, or on the face, hands, feet, or genitals, and for any cough that is severe, bloody, or lasts more than a few weeks. Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. People allergic to bees or bee products should not use honey on skin. Ordinary honey is not sterile; only medical-grade dressings belong on broken skin under clinical guidance.
storage: Store honey for skin use sealed at room temperature; discard any honey dressing once opened past its labeled date, and keep medical dressings in their sealed packaging until use.
evidence_grade: graded: medical-grade honey wound dressings supported as part of proper wound care; honey for cough in people over one year mixed-to-supported for soothing only; honey as a cure for infection, diabetes, or chronic disease unproven
variations: Honey face mask: honey mixed with plain yogurt for unbroken skin, washed off after fifteen minutes.
Honey lip balm: honey blended into a beeswax balm base for dry lips.
Honey bath: honey dissolved in warm bath water for a skin-softening soak.

title: Honey Soap and Skincare: Masks, Balms, and Soap
description: Honey soap and skincare use honey as a humectant, an ingredient that draws and holds moisture, which is why honey appears in masks, lip balms, and soaps rather than as a cleanser on its own. A honey face mask mixes honey with yogurt or oatmeal into a paste that sits on unbroken skin for fifteen minutes and is then rinsed off, leaving skin feeling soft because honey holds water against the surface. A honey lip balm blends a small amount of honey into a beeswax and oil base, so the balm seals moisture in while the honey adds a light sweetness and a smooth texture. Honey soap is made by the cold-process method, where oils and a lye solution are mixed until they thicken, honey is added at a small percentage of the oil weight, and the soap cures for four to six weeks; the honey adds lather and a warm color, and it also heats the soap, so honey soap batches must be watched to prevent overheating and cracking. Soapmaking with lye is an adult project requiring gloves and eye protection, since lye burns skin and eyes.
ingredients: Lye (sodium hydroxide) and water, for soap only
Beeswax and plant oil for balm
Oatmeal and plain yogurt for masks
Gloves, eye protection, soap molds, and a scale
method: For a mask: mix one tablespoon of honey with one tablespoon of yogurt or oatmeal, apply to clean unbroken skin, rest fifteen minutes, and rinse.
For a balm: melt one part beeswax with three parts plant oil, stir in a small spoonful of honey, pour into tins, and cool.
For soap: weigh all ingredients, dissolve lye in water outdoors or under ventilation while wearing gloves and eye protection, and cool to room temperature.
Mix the lye solution into the oils, stir until the mixture thickens to trace, then add honey at about five percent of the oil weight and stir well.
Pour into molds, insulate lightly, watch for overheating, unmold after two days, and cure for four to six weeks before use.
safety: Lye burns skin and eyes: gloves and eye protection are required for soapmaking, and children must stay away from lye. Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Honey skincare is for unbroken skin only; stop if redness or itching appears. Soap is for skin, never for eating.
storage: Store honey soap in a dry, ventilated place so bars harden and last longer; store balm in sealed tins at room temperature for up to three months; mix masks fresh each time.
variations: Oatmeal honey mask: honey, oatmeal, and water for a plain, gentle mask.
Honey shea balm: honey in a shea butter and beeswax base for very dry lips.
Honey lavender soap: honey soap with dried lavender on top, added after pouring.

print("Per bar (%d bars): %.0f g oils, %.1f g honey" % (BARS, OIL_G / BARS, honey / BARS))
print("Soap is for skin, never for eating; keep honey soap dry between uses.")

Per bar (10 bars): 100 g oils, 5.0 g honey

title: Honey in Breads and Cereals: Granola and Honey Bread
description: Honey breads and granola are the everyday end of honey baking, where honey sweetens the dough or binds the cereal and gives both a golden crust and a longer-keeping crumb. Honey bread replaces part or all of the sugar in a bread dough with honey, which feeds the yeast, browns the crust, and keeps the loaf soft for days, but the dough needs a slightly cooler rise, since honey's sugars ferment faster than plain sugar. Granola tosses oats, nuts, and seeds in honey and oil, then bakes the mixture low and slow until crisp, with the honey acting as both sweetener and glue that forms the clusters. The shared technique is low heat and patience: honey burns at high temperatures, so both bread and granola are baked cooler and longer than their sugar versions, and both are cooled fully before cutting or storing so their textures set.
ingredients: Bread flour, yeast, salt, and water for bread
Rolled oats, nuts, seeds, and oil for granola
Dried fruit for granola, added after baking
method: For honey bread: dissolve honey in warm water, add yeast, and rest until foamy.
Mix in flour and salt, knead until smooth, and rise until doubled, about one hour.
Shape into a loaf, rise again for forty minutes, and bake at 350 degrees Fahrenheit until the crust is deep golden.
For granola: toss oats, nuts, and seeds with honey and oil until evenly coated.
Bake at 300 degrees Fahrenheit, stirring every fifteen minutes, until golden and crisp, then cool fully and stir in dried fruit.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Granola with nuts is a choking hazard for young children; keep nut pieces large enough to avoid, or make a nut-free version for children.
storage: Store honey bread wrapped at room temperature for up to five days, or sliced and frozen for a month; store granola airtight at room temperature for up to four weeks.
variations: Honey oat bread: add rolled oats to the dough for a hearty loaf.
Nut-free granola: use seeds and dried fruit only, with the same honey and oil ratio.
Cinnamon granola: add cinnamon and vanilla to the honey coating before baking.

title: Honey Preservation Science: Low Water Activity, Crystallization, and Reliquification
description: Honey preserves itself because it has very low water activity, a measure of how much water in a food is free for microbes to use, and honey's water activity sits around 0.5 to 0.6, below the level most bacteria and yeasts need to grow. Honey is about eighty percent sugar and seventeen percent water, and the sugar binds the water so tightly that microbes cannot reach it, which is why a sealed jar of honey keeps for years without refrigeration and why archaeologists have found edible honey in ancient jars. Crystallization is the other half of honey science: honey is a supersaturated sugar solution, and over time glucose separates out as crystals, starting from tiny seed crystals or pollen grains and spreading through the jar. Crystallization is not spoilage and does not change the honey's safety or flavor, and it is reversed by gentle warming, which redissolves the crystals without harming the honey, as long as the honey is never heated past about 140 degrees Fahrenheit, where flavor and aroma fade.
ingredients: Honey in a sealed glass jar
A warm-water bath or a warm room
method: Check the honey: if it is cloudy or gritty, it has crystallized, which is normal and safe.
Place the sealed jar in warm water, not boiling water, and keep the water below 140 degrees Fahrenheit.
Stir the honey occasionally as it warms, so the crystals dissolve evenly.
Remove the jar once the honey is clear and liquid again, and dry the outside before storing.
Store the reliquified honey sealed at room temperature; it may crystallize again over time, and the same warming reverses it.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Never heat honey in a sealed airtight container that cannot vent, and never microwave honey in plastic, which can melt or leach. Discard honey that ferments, bubbles, or smells of alcohol, which means water got in.
storage: Store honey sealed at room temperature, away from moisture; honey does not need refrigeration, and refrigeration speeds crystallization.
variations: Fast reliquification: use a warm-water bath and stir often for a large jar.
Slow reliquification: leave the jar in a warm room for a day for a small jar.
Seeded crystallization: stir in finely crystallized honey to make smooth creamed honey deliberately.

demo.code:
TITLE = 'Honey Preservation Science: Low Water Activity, Crystallization, and Reliquification'
WATER_PCT = [15, 17, 19, 21]; JAR_G = 500; CRYST_PCT = 80
for w in WATER_PCT:
    aw = 0.25 + 0.02 * w
    print("Water %.0f%% -> estimated water activity %.2f" % (w, aw))
mins = JAR_G * CRYST_PCT / 100 * 0.05
print("Reliquify %d g jar at %d%% crystallized: about %.0f minutes in warm (not boiling) water" % (JAR_G, CRYST_PCT, mins))
print("Estimates only; water activity below about 0.60 resists most microbial growth.")

Water 17% -> estimated water activity 0.59

title: Honey Varieties and Tasting: Clover, Wildflower, and Manuka
description: Honey varieties take their names from the flowers the bees visited most, and tasting them side by side is the fastest way to learn how much honey flavor varies. Clover honey is light, mild, and gently floral, the classic all-purpose honey that suits tea and baking without dominating them. Wildflower honey is made from many flowers at once, so its flavor changes with the season and the place, ranging from light and grassy to dark and caramel-like, and it is the best variety for tasting the landscape a honey came from. Manuka honey comes from the manuka tree in New Zealand and Australia, and it is marketed at high prices for its antibacterial activity, which is measured as a methylglyoxal level; the evidence for manuka honey in wound care is similar to the evidence for other medical-grade honeys, supported only as part of proper wound care, and claims that manuka honey cures infections or disease are unproven. Tasting is done like wine tasting: look at the color, smell the aroma, taste a small amount neat, and note the finish, since honey flavor lingers. Honey is not a cure for any disease. Nothing in this record diagnoses, treats, or replaces medical care; see a clinician for wounds that are deep, large, infected, slow to heal, or on the face, hands, feet, or genitals, and for any cough that is severe, bloody, or lasts more than a few weeks.
ingredients: Clover honey, wildflower honey, and manuka honey
Small tasting spoons and plain crackers
method: Pour a small amount of each honey into separate dishes and note the color, from pale gold to dark amber.
Smell each honey before tasting, and note floral, grassy, caramel, or herbal aromas.
Taste a small amount neat, let it coat the tongue, and note sweetness, floral character, and finish.
Cleanse the palate with water and a plain cracker between varieties.
Write notes for each honey: color, aroma, sweetness, flavor, and finish, and rank them by preference for tea, baking, and eating neat.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Manuka honey is still honey: it is not for infants under 12 months, and it is not a medicine. Do not pay a premium price for health claims; buy manuka for flavor, and judge it by taste.
storage: Store tasting honeys sealed at room temperature; keep manuka honey sealed and dry like any honey, and note that its price does not change its storage needs.
evidence_grade: graded: manuka honey for wound care supported only as part of proper wound care, like other medical-grade honeys; manuka honey as a cure for infection or disease unproven
variations: Single-origin tasting: compare three wildflower honeys from three places.
Dark honey tasting: compare buckwheat, chestnut, and dark wildflower honeys.
Baking tasting: bake the same cake with clover and with wildflower honey and compare.

title: Honey Storage and Handling: Crystallization Reversal, Containers, and Shelf Life
description: Honey storage is simple because honey preserves itself, but a few handling rules keep it at its best for years. Honey keeps indefinitely in a sealed container at room temperature, since its low water activity and natural acidity resist microbes, and it does not need refrigeration, which actually speeds crystallization. The best containers are glass jars with tight lids, since glass does not absorb odors and does not react with honey's acidity, while plastic is acceptable for short storage but can absorb flavors over time, and metal containers should be avoided for long storage because honey's acidity can react with some metals. Crystallization is the main handling event: over weeks or months, glucose crystals form and the honey turns cloudy and gritty, which is normal, safe, and reversible by warming the sealed jar gently in warm water below 140 degrees Fahrenheit until the honey is clear again. Honey that ferments, bubbles, smells of alcohol, or tastes sour has absorbed water, usually from a wet spoon or an unsealed jar, and should be discarded.
ingredients: A clean, dry spoon for every use
method: Transfer honey to a clean, dry glass jar with a tight lid, and label it with the variety and date.
Store the jar at room temperature in a dark place, away from moisture and strong odors.
Always use a clean, dry spoon, since a wet spoon introduces the water that lets honey ferment.
When the honey crystallizes, warm the sealed jar in a water bath below 140 degrees Fahrenheit, stirring occasionally, until clear.
Check stored honey yearly: clear or crystallized honey is fine, while bubbling, alcoholic-smelling, or sour honey should be discarded.
safety: Honey is not for infants under 12 months, because of the risk of infant botulism. This rule holds for every honey in this record, raw or heated, and for any food or drink made with honey that an infant might eat. Never heat a sealed jar that cannot vent, never microwave honey in plastic, and never feed honey to infants under 12 months, however it is stored.
storage: Store honey sealed at room temperature for years; honey has no fixed expiry date when kept dry and sealed, but flavor is best within two years of harvest.
variations: Bulk storage: keep a large jar sealed and refill a small working jar from it.
Travel storage: carry honey in a small, sealed, leak-proof jar, never in an open container.
Gift storage: bottle honey in small glass jars with labels and a note that crystallization is normal.

    print("%d g jar at %d%% crystallized: about %.0f minutes in a warm-water bath" % (size, CRYST_PCT, mins))
print("Never microwave honey in plastic; never heat past 140 F or flavor fades.")
